questions.q: What is the main practical benefit of using an established backtesting framework instead of a fully hand-rolled engine for everyday research?
options: It guarantees the strategy will be profitable
It eliminates the need to understand how backtests work
It handles error-prone boilerplate like commissions, slippage, order types, and statistics consistently
It removes the need for historical price data
questions.explain: Frameworks remove repetitive, easy-to-get-wrong boilerplate — but they don't remove the need to understand the mechanics or to configure realistic assumptions.

questions.q: In backtesting.py, what does the Strategy class's `next()` method correspond to in the hand-rolled engine from the previous lesson?
options: The vectorized `.shift(1)` call
The body of the event-driven loop that runs once per bar
The final performance statistics calculation
The data download step
questions.explain: backtesting.py is architecturally event-driven: `next()` is called once per bar in chronological order, just like the hand-built `for bar in bars` loop.

questions.q: What is vectorbt's main architectural advantage over an event-driven framework?
options: It can trade stocks that event-driven frameworks cannot
It is vectorized and Numba-accelerated, allowing large parameter sweeps to run near-C speed instead of looping one combination at a time
It eliminates the need to model fees or slippage
It automatically prevents overfitting
questions.explain: vectorbt's vectorized, Numba-accelerated design is particularly suited to running many parameter combinations or many assets at once, much faster than an event-driven loop could.

questions.q: What institutional-grade features does a zipline-style framework add on top of a basic event-driven engine?
options: Nothing — zipline is identical to backtesting.py
Real trading calendars, a cross-sectional Pipeline API for factor computation, and pluggable slippage/commission models
Automatic removal of look-ahead bias that other frameworks cannot achieve
Guaranteed real-time execution with brokers
questions.explain: zipline-style frameworks add conventions useful for realistic multi-asset, institutional-style research: trading calendars, a Pipeline API, and swappable cost models.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what do NONE of these frameworks do for you?
options: Compute an equity curve
Apply a commission to trades
Determine whether your strategy's edge is real or just an overfit artifact of your parameter choices
Plot results
questions.explain: Frameworks remove boilerplate, not responsibility — none of them can tell you whether a backtested edge will hold up out-of-sample or is a product of overfitting, which is the focus of Lesson 19.
